title: ITN 170 Final Review Guide
description: Everything on the final in one place, in the same order as the quiz and flashcards: navigation, file maintenance, permissions, wildcards, monitoring, services, finding files and links, pipes and text tools, users and sudo, vi, cron and scripting, ending with the mix-ups that cost marks.

blocks.text: Where am I, and who am I?
Most mistakes at the command line come from being somewhere, or someone, you did not expect. These commands answer both questions.

rows: Prints the full path of the directory you are in
Prints the account you are logged in as
Lists the files in a directory
Long listing: permissions, owner, group, size, date, name
Long listing, sorted by time, **reversed**: oldest first, newest last
Changes directory; with no argument it goes home
Shows a command's manual page (`q` quits, `/` searches)

blocks.text: The dots

cd ..      # up to the parent directory
cd .       # stay exactly where you are
cd ~       # home
cd -       # back to the previous directory

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: `ls -ltr` is three options bundled together: `-l` long, `-t` by time, `-r` reverse. Because of the reverse, the file you changed most recently is the **last** line, right above your prompt.
Becoming root

rows: Switches to root and loads root's login environment
Runs **one** command with root privileges, if you are allowed to
Uses sudo to start a root shell

blocks.label: Watch out:
blocks.text: A prompt ending in `#` means you are root. Every command you type there runs with full power, so check the prompt before anything destructive.

rows: Creates an empty file, or updates the timestamp of an existing one
Makes a directory (`-p` also makes missing parents)
Copies a file (`-r` for a directory)
Moves a file, or renames it when the destination is in the same directory
Deletes a file; there is no trash can

Same, but forced: no prompts and no complaints about missing files

blocks.text: Changing the properties of a file

blocks.label: Gotcha:
blocks.text: `rmdir` refuses to remove a directory that has anything in it. That is not a bug: it is the safety. `rm -r` is the one that removes contents too, and `rm -rf` is the one that does so without asking.
Reading a long listing

-rwxr-xr--  1  alice  staff  120  Oct 6  backup.sh
|\_/\_/\_/
| |  |  |
| |  |  +-- others: r--  (read only)
| |  +----- group:  r-x  (read and execute)
| +-------- owner:  rwx  (read, write and execute)
+---------- type:   -    (ordinary file; d is a directory)
Octal (numeric) permissions
Each permission has a value: **read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1**. Add the values you want for each of the three groups, owner first.

rows: Private files such as SSH keys
Shared with a group, closed to everyone else

blocks.text: Symbolic mode

chmod u+x script.sh     # add execute for the owner, leave all else alone
chmod g-w file.txt       # take write away from the group
chmod o=r file.txt       # others: read only
chmod a+r file.txt       # everyone gets read

blocks.label: Scripts:
blocks.text: To run `./myscript` the file needs **execute** permission (and read). `bash myscript` only needs read, because bash opens the file rather than executing it.
The shell expands them first
Wildcards are replaced by the shell with matching file names **before** the command runs. Brace expansion is different: it builds names from a list, whether or not any file exists.

rows: One character that is **not** in the set
Builds a list of names (does not search)

blocks.text: Worked example
Suppose the directory holds `project`, `project1` to `project4`, `project12` to `project14`, and `projecta`, `projecte`, `projectg`, `projecth`.

rows: project2, project4, projecta, projecte, projectg, projecth

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: `touch project{1..4} project{12..14} project{a,e,g,h}` creates 4 + 3 + 4 = 11 files. Braces make names; `*` and `?` find names that already exist.
Showing a file's contents

rows: Prints it with the last line first (cat backwards)
One screen at a time; Space for the next page
Pager that scrolls both ways; `j`/`k` or arrows, `/` to search, `q` to quit
Last 10 lines (`-n 3` for 3; `-f` follows new lines)
Simple editor with its commands shown on screen: Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X exits
The standard editor; see the vi section

blocks.text:
head -n 3 notes.txt     # the first three lines
tail -n 3 notes.txt     # the last three
tac notes.txt | head    # the last ten lines, newest first

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: `head` and `tail` both default to **10** lines.

Services with systemctl
`systemctl` replaced the older `service` command in RHEL 7. It controls systemd services and normally needs root.

rows: Enable at boot and start it now, in one go

blocks.text: Looking at the system

rows: A live view of processes with CPU and memory use (`q` quits)
Sends a signal to a process; the default asks it to end, `-9` forces it
Free disk space per file system
Kernel messages: hardware and driver warnings or errors
Disk and CPU I/O statistics, refreshed every second
Network connections, routes and interfaces (older; `ss` and `ip` replace it)
A virtual file describing the CPUs

blocks.label: Gotcha:
blocks.text: `start` and `enable` are different questions: one is about **now**, the other about the **next boot**. An ordinary user can only `kill` their own processes.
find and locate

rows: Walks the real directories every time
Looks names up in a prebuilt database
Only as fresh as the last `updatedb`

blocks.text:
find . -name "notes.txt"             # here and below
find / -name "ifcfg-enp0s3" 2>/dev/null   # whole system, hide the permission errors
locate notes.txt
sudo updatedb                            # refresh locate's database
Hard links and soft links

rows: A second name for the **same data**
A tiny file holding the **path** to the original
Still works; the data lives until the last name goes

blocks.text:
ln original.txt copy.txt       # hard link
ln -s /etc/hosts hostslink      # soft link
ls -l hostslink                 # shows:  hostslink -> /etc/hosts

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: A soft link is like a shortcut. A hard link is like giving the same file two names.

rows: Sends output to a file, **replacing** its contents
**Appends** output to the end of a file
Feeds one command's output into the next

blocks.text: The text toolkit

rows: Prints lines that match (`-c` counts, `-i` ignores case)
Sorts lines (`-n` numeric, `-r` reverse, `-k2` by column 2)
Works field by field: `$1` first, `$2` second
Writes to a file **and** to the screen

blocks.text: Putting it together
Take a file called `pets` with a name and a kind on each line:

Rex Dog
Tom Cat
Fido Dog
Kit Cat
Max Dog

awk '{print $2}' pets | sort | uniq -c
#   2 Cat
#   3 Dog

blocks.label: Why sort first?
blocks.text: `uniq` only compares each line with the one **before** it. Sorting puts identical lines side by side, so `sort | uniq -c` counts every group correctly.
Account commands

rows: Creates an account (`adduser` is the same on RHEL/CentOS)
Sets a password; a new account stays locked until you do
Starts a login session as that user (`exit` comes back)

blocks.text: Giving someone sudo rights
On CentOS and RHEL, members of the **wheel** group may run any command as root through sudo.

sudo su                       # 1. become root
useradd newuser               # 2. create the account
passwd newuser                # 3. set a password
usermod -aG wheel newuser     # 4. add to wheel
su - newuser                  # 5. switch to the new user
sudo whoami                   #    prints: root

blocks.label: Never forget the -a:
blocks.text: `usermod -G wheel newuser` **replaces** all the user's supplementary groups with just wheel. `-aG` **appends**, which is what you want.

blocks.label: Which password?
blocks.text: sudo asks for the password of the person typing, not root's. The rules come from `/etc/sudoers`, which you edit with `visudo`; on RHEL it grants the wheel group full access.
Modes
vi opens in **command mode**, where every key is a command. That is why typing seems to do nothing at first. Press `i` to enter **insert mode** and type; press `Esc` to go back.

rows: Replace the character under the cursor
Delete the character under the cursor
Search forward (`n` for the next match)
Save and quit (`ZZ` is Shift+Z twice)

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: The `!` in `:q!` means "even though there are unsaved changes". If you only want to leave a file you did not change, `:q` is enough.

blocks.text: Managing your crontab

rows: Edit your jobs (opens vi by default)

blocks.label: Gotcha:
blocks.text: Minute comes **first**, then hour: `15 6 * * 1` is 6:15 a.m. on Mondays, not 15:06. The third field is the day of the **month**.
The basics

items: Any command you can type at the prompt can go into a script.
The first line, `#!/bin/bash`, is the **shebang**: it names the interpreter that runs the file.
Run it with `bash myscript.sh` (needs read) or `./myscript.sh` (needs execute, after `chmod +x`).

blocks.text: if

if [ -f /etc/passwd ]; then
  echo "found it"
fi                       # closes an if
for

for name in alice bob carol; do
  echo "Hello, $name"
done                     # closes a loop
case

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: Spaces matter inside `[ ... ]`. Each block closes with its keyword backwards or its own word: `if` ends with `fi`, `case` with `esac`, loops with `done`.
Pairs that are easy to confuse

rows: Up one level vs stay where you are
Replace the file vs append to it
Empty directories only vs a directory and everything in it
Become root (root's password) vs run one command as root (your password)
Run now vs run at boot
Replace the groups vs add to them
Another name for the same data vs a shortcut that can break
Live search vs a database that may be stale
First lines vs last lines (10 by default)
Zero or more characters vs exactly one
Builds four names vs matches one of four existing characters
Oldest first, newest last (the `-r` reverses newest-first)
Needs read permission vs needs execute permission
Minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, in that order
